stem: A farmer who ingested an organophosphate insecticide has bradycardia, miosis, bronchorrhoea, wheeze and sweating. How should atropine be administered?

options.B: Doubling IV boluses (e.g. 1–3 mg) every 5 minutes until atropinised, then an infusion
options.D: Titrate atropine to fully dilated pupils and a heart rate above 120/min
options.E: Avoid atropine if tachycardia develops at any point, even with bronchorrhoea

explanation: Atropine antagonises muscarinic effects and is titrated by dose-doubling until atropinisation endpoints (clear chest on auscultation, heart rate above 80, SBP above 80, dry axillae, pupils no longer pinpoint), then maintained at about 10–20% of the loading dose per hour. Tachycardia is not a contraindication, as it may result from hypoxia or hypovolaemia.

stem: What is the current evidence regarding pralidoxime in organophosphorus pesticide poisoning?

options.A: It replaces the need for atropine
options.B: It is contraindicated in all cases
options.C: It is proven to halve mortality in all organophosphate poisoning, whatever the compound ingested
options.D: No clear mortality benefit in trials, though it reactivates AChE for some agents; use varies
options.E: It is only effective when given after 72 hours

explanation: Oximes reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before "ageing" occurs. The randomised trial by Eddleston et al. found no benefit and a trend to harm, despite reactivation, though effectiveness varies by pesticide. Atropine, airway management and supportive care remain essential.
referenceText: Eddleston et al. 2008 (organophosphorus poisoning) [58]; Eddleston et al. 2009 (pralidoxime RCT) [59]

stem: Two days after apparent recovery from cholinergic crisis, a patient with organophosphate poisoning develops weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs and cranial nerves with respiratory failure. What is this?

options.B: Intermediate syndrome

explanation: Intermediate syndrome occurs 24–96 hours after poisoning, after the cholinergic phase, with proximal, neck flexor, cranial nerve and respiratory muscle weakness. It responds poorly to atropine and requires ventilatory support. Delayed polyneuropathy appears after 1–3 weeks with distal weakness.

stem: Which neuromuscular blocker should be avoided during intubation of a patient with organophosphate poisoning?

options.B: Suxamethonium

explanation: Suxamethonium is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase, which is inhibited by organophosphates, causing prolonged paralysis (hours). Non-depolarising agents such as rocuronium are preferred, although higher doses may be needed.
referenceText: Eddleston et al. 2008 (organophosphorus poisoning) [58]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

stem: A young adult ingested an aluminium phosphide tablet (rice/grain fumigant) and presents with profound refractory shock, metabolic acidosis and a garlic-like odour. Which statement about management is correct?

options.B: Most patients recover with oral fluids alone
options.D: No specific antidote; supportive care, vasopressors and consideration of ECMO
options.E: Gastric lavage with water is essential and harmless in all patients after ingestion

explanation: Aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, causing myocardial toxicity, refractory shock and high mortality. Care is supportive; magnesium, glucose–insulin and other agents have been tried without proven benefit, and VA-ECMO has been used successfully. Water may increase phosphine release; staff should avoid exposure.

stem: A patient presents 6 hours after a single paracetamol overdose with a level above the treatment line. Which acetylcysteine regimen is recommended in the 2020 Australian and New Zealand guideline?

options.B: Acetylcysteine only if liver function tests are abnormal at 24 hours
options.C: Two-bag regimen: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h

explanation: The two-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 h then 100 mg/kg over 16 h) reduces adverse reactions compared with the traditional three-bag regimen while being equally effective. Treatment should be started within 8 hours of ingestion for maximal efficacy.

stem: A patient took multiple paracetamol doses over 36 hours (staggered overdose), totalling more than 10 g. How should the nomogram be applied?

options.B: Use the 4-hour line based on the first dose
options.C: Do not treat if the current paracetamol level is below 150 mg/L at the time of presentation
options.E: The nomogram cannot be used; start acetylcysteine and check level and ALT

explanation: Nomograms only apply to single acute ingestions with a known time. For staggered or supratherapeutic ingestions, acetylcysteine is started if the ingested dose exceeds thresholds, with decisions to stop based on paracetamol concentration and ALT after the treatment course.

stem: A patient has a paracetamol level more than twice the treatment line after a massive ingestion. Which adjustment is recommended?

options.A: Increase the acetylcysteine dose (e.g. double the second bag) and seek toxicology advice
options.B: Start haemodialysis in all cases
options.C: Avoid acetylcysteine, because of the risk of fluid overload and hyponatraemia at high doses
options.D: Use the standard regimen without modification

explanation: Massive ingestions (e.g. paracetamol concentrations above double the nomogram line) overwhelm standard acetylcysteine dosing; the Australian guideline recommends increasing the dose in the second infusion. Very high levels with coma and lactic acidosis may require haemodialysis.
referenceText: Chiew et al. 2020 (paracetamol poisoning guideline) [36]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A patient with amitriptyline overdose has seizures, hypotension and QRS duration of 140 ms. What is the first-line treatment for the cardiac toxicity?

options.B: IV sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg, targeting pH 7.45–7.55
options.D: Physostigmine to reverse the anticholinergic effects

explanation: TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, prolonging the QRS. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate overcomes the blockade and alkalinises, reducing drug binding. Class IA and IC antiarrhythmics worsen toxicity, physostigmine may cause asystole, and flumazenil can provoke seizures.

stem: A patient with propranolol overdose has bradycardia and hypotension unresponsive to fluids, atropine and calcium. Which therapy is recommended?

options.B: Sodium nitroprusside
options.C: High-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy with dextrose and potassium monitoring
options.E: Verapamil infusion to stabilise conduction, with temporary transvenous pacing

explanation: High-dose insulin improves myocardial carbohydrate use and contractility in beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning. Glucagon, vasopressors, pacing, lipid emulsion and ECMO are other options. Propranolol also blocks sodium channels and may need bicarbonate.

stem: A patient with sustained-release verapamil overdose has hypotension, bradycardia and hyperglycaemia. Which combination is most appropriate?

options.B: Fomepizole
options.C: IV calcium, high-dose insulin and vasopressors, considering whole bowel irrigation
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate alone, as for tricyclic antidepressant toxicity with a broad QRS complex

explanation: CCBs inhibit L-type channels in myocardium, vasculature and pancreatic islets, causing hyperglycaemia (a marker of severity). Treatment includes calcium salts, high-dose insulin, catecholamines and, for refractory shock, ECMO. Whole bowel irrigation may reduce absorption of sustained-release preparations.

stem: Which feature is an indication for digoxin-specific antibody fragments in acute digoxin poisoning?

options.B: Mild nausea alone
options.C: Potassium above 5.0 mmol/L or a life-threatening arrhythmia
options.E: Serum digoxin of 1.5 ng/mL without symptoms at 2 hours

explanation: Indications for Fab fragments include life-threatening dysrhythmias, hyperkalaemia above 5.0 mmol/L in acute poisoning, end-organ dysfunction, and very high levels or ingestions. Calcium for hyperkalaemia in digoxin toxicity is controversial; Fab treats both the arrhythmia and hyperkalaemia.

stem: Which patient with lithium poisoning has a recommended indication for haemodialysis according to EXTRIP?

options.A: Lithium 4.5 mmol/L with impaired kidney function, or reduced consciousness, seizures or dysrhythmias
options.B: Lithium 1.5 mmol/L with tremor only
options.C: All patients on chronic lithium with diarrhoea
options.D: Lithium 2.0 mmol/L with normal kidney function and no symptoms, 6 hours after an acute-on-chronic overdose

explanation: EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment if lithium exceeds 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function, or with decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias irrespective of concentration. It suggests treatment if levels exceed 5.0 mmol/L, with confusion, or if the expected time to reach below 1.0 mmol/L exceeds 36 hours.

stem: A patient has blurred vision, pH 7.05, anion gap 30 and osmolar gap 35 after drinking illicit spirits. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Fomepizole (or ethanol), haemodialysis, bicarbonate and folinic acid
options.B: Wait for the methanol level before starting any specific treatment or dialysis

explanation: Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid, causing acidosis and retinal toxicity. ADH inhibition with fomepizole or ethanol prevents further metabolism; haemodialysis removes methanol and formate. Folinic acid enhances formate metabolism. Treatment should not await confirmatory levels.

stem: Which finding is characteristic of ethylene glycol poisoning?

options.B: Urinary calcium oxalate crystals with AKI and hypocalcaemia
options.C: Visual loss and optic disc oedema with a raised osmolar gap

explanation: Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids; oxalate binds calcium, causing hypocalcaemia and crystal deposition in kidneys (AKI). Treatment includes fomepizole, haemodialysis, bicarbonate, and thiamine and pyridoxine as cofactors.

stem: A patient rescued from a house fire is comatose and hypotensive with lactate 12 mmol/L. Which antidote is recommended for suspected cyanide toxicity?

options.B: Methylene blue

explanation: Hydrogen cyanide from burning plastics causes mitochondrial poisoning; lactate above 8–10 mmol/L in smoke inhalation suggests significant cyanide toxicity. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin and is preferred, as nitrites induce methaemoglobinaemia, impairing oxygen carriage alongside carbon monoxide.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]; Weaver 2009 (carbon monoxide poisoning) [232]

stem: A patient found unconscious in a room with a charcoal heater has SpO2 99% on pulse oximetry. Why may this reading be misleading?

options.A: CO increases oxygen delivery to tissues
options.B: SpO2 is always accurate in CO poisoning
options.D: Pulse oximetry underestimates oxygen saturation in CO poisoning by about 10 percentage points
options.E: Standard oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin

explanation: Carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhaemoglobin, so standard pulse oximetry overestimates oxygenation. Co-oximetry measures COHb. Treatment is 100% oxygen; hyperbaric oxygen is considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, high COHb, cardiac ischaemia or pregnancy.

stem: Which patient with CO poisoning is most likely to benefit from hyperbaric oxygen?

options.A: A patient with CO exposure 1 week ago and no symptoms
options.B: A patient with mild headache and COHb 5%
options.C: A patient with syncope, neurological deficits or COHb above 25%
options.D: A patient with isolated nausea after 24 hours of 100% oxygen therapy
options.E: A smoker with COHb 8% and no symptoms

explanation: Hyperbaric oxygen accelerates COHb elimination and may reduce delayed neurological sequelae. Weaver et al. showed fewer cognitive sequelae with three HBO sessions in symptomatic CO poisoning. Indications include loss of consciousness, neurological signs, COHb above 25% (above 15–20% in pregnancy), cardiac ischaemia and severe acidosis.

stem: A patient taking sertraline is given tramadol and develops agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible clonus. Which statement is correct?

options.A: This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give bromocriptine and dantrolene, and stop tramadol
options.B: This is malignant hyperthermia; give dantrolene
options.C: This is anticholinergic toxicity; give physostigmine
options.D: This is sepsis; give antibiotics only
options.E: Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity; supportive care, benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine

explanation: Hunter criteria require a serotonergic agent plus spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 °C and clonus. Tramadol, common in misuse in Egypt, has serotonergic activity and lowers seizure threshold.
referenceText: Boyer & Shannon 2005 (serotonin syndrome) [23]; Dunkley et al. 2003 (Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria) [57]

stem: A patient treated with haloperidol develops fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion and CK 25,000 U/L over 3 days. What is the most important first step?

options.B: Stop the antipsychotic and give supportive care, with bromocriptine or dantrolene if severe
options.C: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and continue haloperidol at the current dose

explanation: NMS develops over days with rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and altered mental status due to dopamine D2 blockade. Treatment is withdrawal of the drug, supportive care, benzodiazepines, and bromocriptine or dantrolene in moderate–severe cases. It is distinguished from serotonin syndrome by bradyreflexia and slower onset.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: During general anaesthesia with sevoflurane and suxamethonium, a patient develops rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, masseter rigidity and hyperthermia. What is the specific treatment?

options.A: Increase the volatile anaesthetic concentration to deepen anaesthesia
options.B: Bromocriptine
options.E: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed; stop volatile agents

explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle ryanodine receptors triggered by volatile agents and suxamethonium. Early signs include rising ETCO2 and tachycardia. Management includes stopping triggers, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, dantrolene (2.5 mg/kg, repeated up to 10 mg/kg or more), cooling and treating hyperkalaemia.

stem: A patient presents with agitated delirium, mydriasis, flushed dry skin, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds and tachycardia after ingesting a herbal preparation. Which feature best distinguishes this from sympathomimetic toxicity?

options.B: Mydriasis

explanation: Both anticholinergic and sympathomimetic toxidromes cause tachycardia, mydriasis, hyperthermia and agitation. Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin, urinary retention and reduced bowel sounds, whereas sympathomimetic toxicity causes diaphoresis. Physostigmine may be used for anticholinergic delirium when there are no contraindications (QRS prolongation).

stem: A patient with suspected opioid overdose has respiratory rate 6/min, pinpoint pupils and SpO2 85%, with a pulse. What is the recommended naloxone approach in an opioid-dependent patient?

options.B: Support ventilation and titrate small IV doses (e.g. 0.04–0.1 mg) to restore breathing
options.C: Give 2 mg IV bolus regardless of history
options.D: Avoid naloxone in all opioid-dependent patients because of the risk of precipitating acute withdrawal

explanation: Large naloxone doses in opioid-dependent patients precipitate acute withdrawal, agitation, vomiting and pulmonary oedema. Titrating small doses to adequate ventilation is preferred. Naloxone's duration is shorter than many opioids, so infusions may be needed for long-acting agents such as methadone.

stem: Why is flumazenil generally avoided in undifferentiated overdose with coma?

options.B: It is ineffective against benzodiazepines
options.C: It can precipitate seizures, especially with proconvulsant co-ingestants or dependence
options.D: It has a duration of action of several days, causing prolonged withdrawal and agitation

explanation: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine effects but can provoke seizures and arrhythmias in patients with benzodiazepine dependence or co-ingestion of proconvulsants. It is reasonable for iatrogenic oversedation in benzodiazepine-naive patients.

stem: A patient with valproate overdose has coma and serum ammonia of 180 µmol/L with normal liver enzymes. Which antidote is recommended?

options.B: Flumazenil

explanation: Valproate causes hyperammonaemic encephalopathy by depleting carnitine and inhibiting urea cycle enzymes. L-carnitine is recommended for hyperammonaemia, hepatotoxicity or significant overdose. Haemodialysis is indicated for very high levels (e.g. above 1300 mg/L) or shock and cerebral oedema.

stem: A young woman ingests a large number of ferrous sulfate tablets. She has vomiting, metabolic acidosis, hypotension and serum iron of 110 µmol/L (600 µg/dL) at 4 hours. What is the specific treatment?

options.B: Penicillamine

explanation: Iron is poorly adsorbed by activated charcoal. Deferoxamine chelates free iron and is indicated for systemic toxicity, metabolic acidosis, shock or serum iron above about 90 µmol/L (500 µg/dL). It causes vin rosé urine and, with prolonged infusion, ARDS.

stem: A patient with severe salicylate poisoning becomes confused and is to be intubated. What is a critical consideration during ventilation?

options.A: Set a normal respiratory rate of 12/min
options.B: Stop bicarbonate after intubation
options.D: Maintain high minute ventilation to match prior hyperventilation, avoiding worsening acidosis
options.E: Delay haemodialysis until after extubation to avoid haemodynamic instability during the dialysis run

explanation: Acidaemia increases the non-ionised salicylate fraction, which crosses into the brain. After intubation, relative hypoventilation can precipitate deterioration and arrest. EXTRIP recommends haemodialysis for altered mental status, new hypoxaemia, very high levels (e.g. above 7.2 mmol/L) or failure of standard therapy, alongside urinary alkalinisation.
referenceText: Juurlink et al. 2015 (EXTRIP salicylates) [107]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: For which ingestion is activated charcoal ineffective?

options.B: Quetiapine

explanation: Activated charcoal does not adsorb metals and ions (lithium, iron, potassium), alcohols, acids and alkalis, or hydrocarbons. It is most useful within 1 hour of ingestion of an adsorbable toxin in a patient with a protected airway. Multiple-dose charcoal enhances elimination of carbamazepine, theophylline, phenobarbital, quinine and dapsone.

stem: A young man in Upper Egypt is stung by a scorpion and develops agitation, hypersalivation, sweating, priapism, hypertension and then pulmonary oedema with reduced LVEF. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Autonomic storm with myocardial dysfunction; give supportive care, prazosin and antivenom if indicated
options.B: Atropine should be given routinely to reduce secretions and treat the priapism
options.E: Local wound care alone is sufficient in all cases, because systemic symptoms always resolve spontaneously

explanation: Scorpion venoms (e.g. Leiurus, Androctonus in North Africa) activate sodium channels, releasing catecholamines and acetylcholine. Severe envenoming causes cardiogenic shock and pulmonary oedema, especially in children. Prazosin, dobutamine and supportive ventilation are key; antivenom is used in many regions, though evidence for benefit varies.

stem: A patient bitten by a viper has local swelling and bleeding gums. Blood placed in a clean glass tube fails to clot after 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Specific antivenom, repeating the 20-minute clotting test every 6 hours
options.B: Tourniquet application
options.D: FFP and vitamin K without antivenom, until the clotting test normalises
options.E: Incision and suction of the wound

explanation: The 20-minute whole blood clotting test is a simple bedside test for venom-induced consumption coagulopathy. Antivenom is indicated for systemic envenoming (coagulopathy, bleeding, neurotoxicity, shock, AKI). Blood products do not correct coagulopathy without antivenom; tourniquets and incisions are harmful.

stem: A patient bitten by a cobra develops ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and dysphagia. While antivenom is arranged, which test may identify patients who respond to anticholinesterases?

options.B: Edrophonium without atropine in all patients

explanation: Postsynaptic (elapid) neurotoxins can be partially reversed by anticholinesterases. WHO recommends a neostigmine test with atropine pretreatment; improvement supports continuing neostigmine. Antivenom and airway support remain essential, as respiratory paralysis may develop.

stem: What is the recommended first aid for a snakebite on the leg?

options.A: Application of ice packs for several hours to slow venom absorption and reduce swelling
options.B: Electric shock to the bite site
options.C: Incision and suction of the bite
options.D: Reassurance, limb immobilisation and rapid transport, avoiding tight tourniquets
options.E: Tight arterial tourniquet above the bite

explanation: WHO first aid emphasises reassurance, immobilisation (splinting), removal of tight items and rapid transport. Tourniquets, incisions, suction, ice and electrical shock cause harm without benefit. Pressure-bandage immobilisation is advised for elapid bites without local necrosis in some regions.

stem: A soldier collapses during exercise in hot weather with core temperature 42 °C, confusion and seizures. What is the most effective cooling method?

options.A: Cold-water immersion to rapidly lower core temperature toward 39 °C
options.B: Slow evaporative cooling over 6 hours to avoid shivering and rebound

explanation: Exertional heat stroke is defined by core temperature above 40 °C with CNS dysfunction. Rapid cooling within 30 minutes reduces mortality; cold-water immersion achieves the fastest cooling rates. Antipyretics are ineffective because the hypothalamic set point is normal; dantrolene is not recommended.

stem: Which complication is commonly associated with severe heat stroke?

options.B: Hypercalcaemia
options.C: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC and acute liver injury

explanation: Heat stroke causes direct cellular injury and a systemic inflammatory response leading to multiorgan dysfunction: rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, liver injury (transaminases peak at 24–72 hours), ARDS and encephalopathy. Classic (non-exertional) heat stroke affects elderly people during heatwaves.

stem: A patient with core temperature 30 °C has a pulse and stable haemodynamics. Which rewarming strategy is appropriate?

options.A: Active external and minimally invasive rewarming (forced air, warmed fluids) with gentle handling
options.B: Immersion in hot water at 45 °C
options.C: No active rewarming; allow passive spontaneous rewarming over 24 hours in a cool room
options.E: ECMO rewarming as first-line in all patients

explanation: Moderate hypothermia (28–32 °C) with stable circulation is treated with active external and minimally invasive rewarming. Extracorporeal rewarming is reserved for cardiac arrest or instability. Rough handling may precipitate VF.

stem: A worker sustained a high-voltage electrical injury with small entry and exit burns. What is the most important consideration?

options.B: Fluid resuscitation should follow the Parkland formula, based only on the visible skin burn area
options.D: Deep tissue damage may be extensive despite small burns, risking rhabdomyolysis and arrhythmias
options.E: Skin burn size accurately predicts fluid needs

explanation: High-voltage current travels along low-resistance tissues (nerves, vessels, muscle), causing deep necrosis disproportionate to surface burns. Monitoring for arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis (high urine output targets), compartment syndrome and spinal injury is required; fluid needs exceed skin-burn-based estimates.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient ingested a concentrated alkaline drain cleaner 2 hours ago and has drooling and odynophagia. Which management is appropriate?

options.B: Activated charcoal
options.C: Give oral vinegar to neutralise the alkali, followed by milk to dilute it and protect the mucosa
options.E: Airway assessment, nil by mouth, and endoscopy or CT within 12–48 hours; no emesis or neutralisation

explanation: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis, particularly of the oesophagus. Emesis, neutralisation and charcoal are contraindicated. Early airway evaluation, CT and endoscopy (typically within 12–48 hours) grade injury and guide management; perforation requires surgery.

stem: Which management principle is specific to paraquat poisoning?

options.B: High-flow oxygen to maintain SpO2 at 100% from presentation, to protect the lungs
options.C: Avoid supplemental oxygen unless hypoxaemic, as oxygen worsens lung injury

explanation: Paraquat generates reactive oxygen species via redox cycling, causing pulmonary fibrosis. High oxygen concentrations accelerate lung injury. Prognosis is poor after significant ingestion; management is supportive with early decontamination.

stem: A patient on tuberculosis treatment ingests a large amount of isoniazid and develops refractory seizures and severe lactic acidosis. What is the specific antidote?

options.B: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6), gram for gram with the isoniazid, or 5 g if unknown
options.E: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV as the first-line anticonvulsant for these seizures

explanation: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxal 5-phosphate, reducing GABA synthesis and causing seizures refractory to standard anticonvulsants. Pyridoxine with benzodiazepines terminates seizures; the lactic acidosis is largely seizure-related.

stem: Which treatment enhances elimination in severe theophylline toxicity with seizures and arrhythmias?

options.A: Haemodialysis or haemoperfusion, plus multiple-dose charcoal
options.B: Urinary alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate infusion

explanation: Theophylline toxicity causes vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, hypokalaemia and seizures. Multiple-dose activated charcoal increases clearance; extracorporeal removal is indicated for seizures, life-threatening arrhythmias or very high levels.

stem: A young woman who used MDMA at a party is confused with sodium 121 mmol/L. What is the mechanism?

options.B: Hyperglycaemia
options.D: Renal salt wasting from diuretic co-ingestion
options.E: Increased ADH secretion plus excessive water intake

explanation: MDMA stimulates ADH release, and users often drink large volumes of water, causing acute hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema, especially in women. Symptomatic patients need hypertonic saline. MDMA also causes hyperthermia, serotonin toxicity and rhabdomyolysis.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]; Spasovski et al. 2014 (European hyponatraemia guideline) [201]

stem: An asymptomatic cocaine body packer has multiple intact packets on CT. What is the preferred management?

options.B: Laxatives containing paraffin oil to dissolve the packets more quickly and speed transit
options.C: Conservative management with whole bowel irrigation, surgery if rupture or obstruction

explanation: Most asymptomatic body packers are managed with whole bowel irrigation and close monitoring until packets pass. Endoscopic removal risks rupture. Signs of cocaine toxicity (packet rupture) or bowel obstruction require surgery, as toxicity from ruptured packets can be fatal.

stem: Why should a paracetamol level be measured in all patients presenting with intentional overdose, even when paracetamol ingestion is denied?

options.A: It replaces the need for liver tests
options.B: Poisoning is common, early symptoms are absent, and early treatment is effective
options.C: It is required to calculate the osmolar gap
options.E: Paracetamol causes immediate coma in most cases of significant overdose, aiding diagnosis

explanation: Early paracetamol toxicity is often asymptomatic, histories are unreliable and delayed treatment increases liver failure risk. Routine paracetamol screening in intentional overdose identifies patients who need acetylcysteine.
referenceText: Chiew et al. 2020 (paracetamol poisoning guideline) [36]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: Which measure protects staff when managing a patient with significant dermal organophosphate exposure?

options.A: Removing contaminated clothing and washing the skin while using gloves and gowns
options.B: Giving prophylactic atropine to staff
options.C: No precautions are needed because organophosphates are not absorbed through skin
options.D: Gastric lavage of the patient in all cases
options.E: Applying alcohol to the patient's skin

explanation: Organophosphates are absorbed through skin; contaminated clothing should be removed and skin washed with soap and water. Staff should use personal protective equipment. Gastric lavage has no proven benefit and risks aspiration.

stem: How does carbamate insecticide poisoning differ from organophosphate poisoning?

options.A: Carbamates bind acetylcholinesterase reversibly, so toxicity is shorter and oximes rarely needed
options.B: Atropine is contraindicated in carbamate poisoning
options.D: Carbamates cross the blood–brain barrier more than organophosphates in all cases and need oximes

explanation: Carbamates cause a cholinergic crisis similar to organophosphates but carbamylate acetylcholinesterase reversibly without ageing, leading to shorter duration. Atropine is the mainstay; oximes are rarely needed.
referenceText: Eddleston et al. 2008 (organophosphorus poisoning) [58]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: Which finding is an indication for haemodialysis in methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?

options.A: Any detectable level in all patients
options.B: Normal pH with a low level after fomepizole has been given and the patient is asymptomatic
options.C: Severe acidosis, visual impairment (methanol) or AKI (ethylene glycol)

explanation: Haemodialysis removes the parent alcohol and toxic metabolites and corrects acidosis. Indications include severe acidosis, end-organ damage (visual disturbance, AKI), very high concentrations, and deterioration despite therapy. Fomepizole alone may suffice for low-level ingestions without acidosis.

stem: Which complication of tramadol overdose is particularly common and may occur even without opioid toxidrome?

options.B: Bradycardia with heart block

explanation: Tramadol inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake and has weak mu-opioid activity. Overdose causes seizures (often early), serotonin toxicity, CNS and respiratory depression. Naloxone reverses opioid effects but may not prevent seizures; benzodiazepines are used for seizures.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]; Boyer & Shannon 2005 (serotonin syndrome) [23]

stem: For which poisoning is intravenous lipid emulsion most established as rescue therapy?

options.B: Carbon monoxide poisoning with coma and myocardial injury

explanation: Lipid emulsion acts as a "lipid sink" and may improve cardiac energetics. Evidence is strongest for local anaesthetic toxicity; it is also used as rescue therapy for refractory lipophilic drug toxicity (e.g. some calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, TCAs), though evidence is weaker and it interferes with laboratory tests and ECMO circuits.

stem: A conscious, shivering patient with core temperature 33 °C is found after outdoor exposure. How is this hypothermia classified?

options.B: Mild hypothermia

explanation: Hypothermia is classified as mild (32–35 °C, shivering, conscious), moderate (28–32 °C, impaired consciousness, shivering may stop), severe (below 28 °C, unconscious) and profound (below about 24 °C). The Swiss staging system uses clinical signs when core temperature cannot be measured.

stem: During antivenom infusion, a patient develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension. What is the immediate management?

options.B: Give atropine
options.C: Abandon antivenom permanently in all cases, giving corticosteroids and antihistamines instead
options.D: Stop the infusion, give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg and fluids; restart cautiously once stable
options.E: Continue antivenom at a faster rate

explanation: Early anaphylactic reactions to antivenom are common. WHO recommends stopping the infusion, IM adrenaline, antihistamines and hydrocortisone, then restarting antivenom slowly if envenoming remains life-threatening. Adrenaline must always be prepared before administration.
referenceText: WHO 2016 (snakebite management) [240]; Cardona et al. 2020 (WAO anaphylaxis guidance) [30]
